q: Joan's husband died in Year 1. She has not remarried, and her 8-year-old son, whom she claims as a dependent, has lived with her in the home she maintains every year since. What is the most advantageous filing status available to Joan for Year 3?
choices: Married filing jointly
Head of household
Single
Qualifying surviving spouse
exp: A surviving spouse who maintains a home for a dependent child may use qualifying surviving spouse status (joint-return rates) for the two years after the year of death, which are Years 2 and 3. Head of household is available only after that period ends.

q: Kay is unmarried and has no children. Her widowed mother lives in a nursing home, and Kay pays more than half the cost of the nursing home and of her mother's support. Her mother has no gross income. What is Kay's most advantageous filing status?
choices: Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
Married filing separately
exp: A dependent parent is a qualifying person for head of household even if the parent does not live with the taxpayer, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of the parent's home (including a nursing home). The usual requirement that the qualifying person live with the taxpayer does not apply to a parent.

q: Lana's divorce became final on December 31 of the current year. She has no children or other dependents. What is her filing status for the current year?
choices: Married filing jointly
Married filing separately
Single
Head of household
exp: Marital status is determined on the last day of the tax year, so a taxpayer divorced on December 31 is unmarried for the entire year and, without a qualifying person, files as single. Married statuses are unavailable once the final decree is entered.

q: Mona is still legally married, but her husband moved out in March and has not lived in the home since. Mona paid all the costs of the home, where her 10-year-old daughter, her dependent, lived with her all year. Her husband refuses to file a joint return. What is Mona's most advantageous filing status?
choices: Married filing separately
Single
Head of household
Qualifying surviving spouse
exp: A married taxpayer is considered unmarried if the spouse was not in the home during the last six months of the year and the taxpayer maintains a home for a dependent child, so Mona may file as head of household. Single status is never available to someone legally married at year-end.

q: Ned and Olga's daughter, age 22, was a full-time college student for nine months of the year and lived at home except while at school. She earned $15,000 from part-time jobs but did not provide more than half of her own support. Can her parents claim her as a dependent?
choices: Yes, as a qualifying child; her gross income does not matter
No, because her gross income exceeds the qualifying relative limit
No, because she is over age 19
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
exp: A full-time student under 24 meets the qualifying child age test, and there is no gross income test for a qualifying child. The gross income limit applies only to qualifying relatives, which is the tempting trap.

q: Pam provides more than half the support of her widowed father, who lives in his own apartment. During the year he received $6,000 of taxable interest and $10,000 of Social Security benefits, none of which is taxable. Assume the qualifying relative gross income limit is $5,200. Can Pam claim her father as a dependent?
choices: No, because his $6,000 of taxable interest exceeds the gross income limit
Yes, because only taxable Social Security counts and his is $0
No, because his $16,000 of total receipts exceeds the gross income limit
Yes, because a parent is exempt from the gross income test
exp: The gross income test counts only items includible in gross income, so nontaxable Social Security is ignored, but the $6,000 of taxable interest alone exceeds the $5,200 limit. Counting all $16,000 reaches the right conclusion for the wrong reason.

q: Rose, age 80, is supported by her three children and herself: Ann provides 35%, Bob 30%, Cal 25%, and Rose 10% from her own savings. Rose has no gross income and meets the other dependency tests. Who may claim Rose as a dependent?
choices: Only Ann, because she provided the most support
Any one of the three children, if the other two sign statements agreeing not to claim her
No one, because no individual provided more than half of her support
Ann or Bob only, because each provided at least 30% of her support
exp: Under a multiple support agreement, any member of a group that together provides more than half the support may claim the dependent if that person provides over 10% and the other over-10% contributors consent. All three children exceed 10%, so any one may be designated.

q: Sam, age 12, is his parents' dependent and has $5,000 of interest and dividend income and no earned income. Assume the dependent standard deduction is $1,350 and the kiddie tax applies to net unearned income above $2,700. How much of Sam's income is taxed at his parents' marginal rate?
exp: Net unearned income is unearned income less twice the $1,350 amount: $5,000 - $2,700 = $2,300, which is taxed at the parents' rate. Subtracting only the standard deduction gives $3,650.

q: Tia, a single taxpayer, is 67 years old and legally blind. Assume the basic standard deduction for a single filer is $15,000 and the additional standard deduction for age or blindness is $2,000 for each condition. Ignore any other deductions for seniors. What is Tia's standard deduction?
exp: A single taxpayer adds the additional amount once for being 65 or older and once for blindness: $15,000 + 2 x $2,000 = $19,000. Allowing only one additional amount gives $17,000.

q: Uri, a single taxpayer, has taxable income of $60,000, all ordinary income. Assume the rates are 10% on taxable income up to $11,925, 12% from $11,925 to $48,475, and 22% from $48,475 to $103,350. What is Uri's regular income tax?

Vic, a single taxpayer, has taxable income of $60,000, which includes $20,000 of qualified dividends; the rest is ordinary income. Assume the 0% rate on qualified dividends applies to taxable income up to $48,350 and the 15% rate applies above that. What is the tax on Vic's qualified dividends?
exp: Ordinary income of $40,000 fills the bottom brackets first; dividends from $40,000 to $48,350 ($8,350) are taxed at 0% and the remaining $11,650 at 15%, or $1,747.50. Taxing all $20,000 at 15% gives $3,000.

q: Wes's prior-year return showed AGI of $200,000 and total tax of $30,000. He expects current-year tax of $50,000. What is the minimum total amount of withholding and timely estimated payments Wes must make to avoid an underpayment penalty?
exp: Required payments are the lesser of 90% of current-year tax ($45,000) or 100% of prior-year tax, increased to 110% when prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000 (110% x $30,000 = $33,000). Using 100% of the prior year gives $30,000.

q: Yara, a single taxpayer, has modified AGI of $230,000, which includes $50,000 of net investment income. The net investment income tax threshold for single filers is $200,000. What is Yara's net investment income tax?
exp: The 3.8% tax applies to the lesser of net investment income ($50,000) or modified AGI over the threshold ($30,000): 3.8% x $30,000 = $1,140. Applying 3.8% to all $50,000 gives $1,900.

q: Zane and Zelda file jointly. Zane earned wages of $180,000 and Zelda earned wages of $120,000 from separate employers, and neither employer withheld additional Medicare tax. The additional Medicare tax threshold is $250,000 for joint filers and the employer withholding threshold is $200,000 per employee. What is their additional Medicare tax liability?
exp: The 0.9% tax applies to combined wages over the $250,000 joint threshold: 0.9% x $50,000 = $450, payable on the return even though no employer withheld it. Using the $200,000 withholding threshold gives $900.

q: Rita and Sam are married and file separate returns. Rita itemizes deductions of $8,000. Sam's itemized deductions total $2,000. Assume the standard deduction for married filing separately is $15,000. What deduction from AGI may Sam claim?
exp: When one spouse filing separately itemizes, the other spouse's standard deduction is zero, so Sam must itemize and deducts his $2,000. Claiming the $15,000 standard deduction is not allowed.

q: Tina, age 7, lives all year with her mother (AGI $30,000) and her grandmother (AGI $50,000). Tina is a qualifying child of both, and both claim her as a dependent on their returns. Under the tie-breaker rules, who is entitled to claim Tina?
choices: The mother, because a parent has priority over a nonparent
The grandmother, because her AGI is higher
Whoever files first
Neither, because Tina is a qualifying child of two taxpayers
exp: When a parent and a nonparent both claim the same qualifying child, the parent wins. The higher-AGI rule applies only when no parent claims the child (or between two parents, by residence then AGI).

q: Una is divorced and has custody of her son all year. She signs a written release allowing her former husband to claim the son as a dependent. Which of the following tax benefits may the former husband claim for the son?
choices: The child tax credit
Head of household filing status
The earned income credit
The child and dependent care credit
exp: A release of the dependency claim lets the noncustodial parent claim the child as a dependent and take the child tax credit. Head of household status, the earned income credit and the dependent care credit stay with the custodial parent because they depend on where the child lives.

q: Vera, age 20, a full-time student, married during the year. She and her husband filed a joint return solely to obtain a $400 refund of income tax withheld; neither would have had a tax liability on separate returns. Her parents meet all other tests to claim her. May her parents claim Vera as a dependent?
choices: Yes, because the joint return was filed only to claim a refund and no tax liability would exist on separate returns
No, because a married individual who files a joint return can never be claimed as a dependent
No, because a full-time student over 19 cannot be a qualifying child
Yes, but only if the parents also provide over half of her husband's support
exp: The joint return test is not violated when the joint return is filed only to claim a refund and no tax liability would exist for either spouse on separate returns. Students under 24 can still be qualifying children.

q: Will, a single taxpayer, had wages of $70,000, taxable interest of $2,000 and a $5,000 long-term capital loss with no capital gains. He made a $4,000 deductible traditional IRA contribution. What is Will's adjusted gross income?
exp: AGI is $70,000 + $2,000 - $3,000 (net capital loss deduction limit) - $4,000 IRA deduction = $65,000, with $2,000 of capital loss carried forward. Deducting the full $5,000 loss gives $63,000.

q: Xia is unmarried and provides all the support for her cousin, who lived with Xia as a member of her household for the entire year and has no gross income. What is Xia's filing status?
choices: Head of household, because she supports a dependent who lives with her
Single, because a cousin who qualifies as a dependent only by living in her household is not a qualifying person for head of household
Head of household, because the cousin has no gross income
Single, because a cousin can never be claimed as a dependent
exp: Xia can claim the cousin as a qualifying relative under the member-of-household test, but a dependent who qualifies only through that test is not a qualifying person for head of household. Assuming every dependent supports head of household status is the trap.

q: Yale, age 20, is a full-time student. His support for the year was $25,000: $12,000 of tuition paid by a scholarship, $8,000 paid by his parents and $5,000 from his summer job earnings. He lives with his parents when not at school. Is Yale his parents' qualifying child?
choices: No, because his own earnings plus his scholarship exceed half of his support
Yes, because a scholarship received by a full-time student is not counted in determining whether he provided over half of his own support
No, because his parents did not provide over half of his total support
Yes, because there is no support test for a qualifying child
exp: Scholarships of a full-time student are disregarded for the self-support test, so Yale provided only $5,000 of $13,000; he did not provide over half his own support. A qualifying child does have a support test (the child must not self-support), and the parents need not provide over half.

q: Zoe, a single taxpayer in the 37% bracket, sold gold coins she had held for three years at a $10,000 gain. She has no other capital transactions. What is the maximum federal income tax on the gain, ignoring the net investment income tax?
exp: Long-term gain on collectibles is taxed at a maximum 28% rate: 28% x $10,000 = $2,800. Applying the 20% maximum rate for other long-term capital gains gives $2,000.

q: Amy's husband died in March of the current year. She has not remarried and has no children or other dependents. What are Amy's filing statuses for the current year and the following year?
choices: Married filing jointly for the current year; single for the following year
Single for both years
Married filing jointly for the current year; qualifying surviving spouse for the following year
Head of household for both years
exp: A surviving spouse may file jointly for the year of death; afterward, qualifying surviving spouse status requires a dependent child, so Amy files as single the next year. Choosing qualifying surviving spouse overlooks the dependent child requirement.

q: Ben, age 16, is his parents' dependent. He earned $8,000 of wages and $1,000 of interest. Assume the dependent standard deduction is the greater of $1,350 or earned income plus $450, not to exceed the regular standard deduction of $15,000. What is Ben's taxable income?
exp: His standard deduction is $8,000 + $450 = $8,450, so taxable income is $9,000 - $8,450 = $550. Using the full $15,000 standard deduction available to non-dependents gives $0.

q: Cara is a U.S. citizen. She provides all the support for her mother, a citizen and resident of Mexico who has never lived in the United States and has no gross income. May Cara claim her mother as a dependent?
choices: No, because a dependent must be a U.S. citizen or resident
No, because a parent must live with the taxpayer to be a qualifying relative
Yes, but only if her mother becomes a U.S. resident before year-end
Yes, because a resident of Mexico meets the citizenship or residency test
exp: The citizenship or residency test is met by U.S. citizens, nationals and residents, and by residents of Canada or Mexico. A parent need not live with the taxpayer to be a qualifying relative.

q: Dale has net earnings from self-employment of $50,000 from his sole proprietorship and no wages. Assume self-employment tax is 15.3% of 92.35% of net earnings. What is Dale's self-employment tax?
exp: SE tax is $50,000 x 92.35% x 15.3% = $7,065 (rounded). Applying 15.3% to the full $50,000 ignores the 92.35% adjustment and gives $7,650; $3,532 is only the deductible half.

q: Eve's son, age 30, is permanently and totally disabled and lives with her all year. He earns $7,000 at a sheltered workshop and does not provide over half of his own support. Assume the qualifying relative gross income limit is $5,200. May Eve claim her son as a dependent?
choices: No, because he is over the age limit for a qualifying child
No, because his gross income exceeds the qualifying relative limit
Yes, as a qualifying child, because the age test does not apply to a permanently and totally disabled child
Yes, but only as a qualifying relative
exp: A permanently and totally disabled child meets the qualifying child age test at any age, and qualifying children have no gross income test. Testing him as a qualifying relative would fail the $5,200 gross income limit.

q: Fay, unmarried, lives with her dependent 9-year-old daughter. The household's costs for the year were rent $12,000, utilities $3,000, groceries consumed in the home $6,000, clothing $2,000 and medical care $1,000. Fay paid $12,000 of these costs and her parents paid the rest. What is the cost of maintaining the household, and does Fay qualify for head of household status?
choices: $21,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
$24,000; she does not qualify because she paid only half
$15,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
$23,000; she qualifies because she paid more than half
exp: Household costs include rent, utilities and food eaten in the home ($21,000) but not clothing or medical care, so Fay's $12,000 is more than half. Including all $24,000 makes her share exactly half, which would fail the more-than-half test.

q: Gil and Hope filed a joint return. After the IRS assessed additional tax attributable to Gil's unreported business income, Hope asked who is liable. Absent innocent spouse relief, what is the rule for joint filers?
choices: Each spouse is liable only for tax on his or her own income
Liability is split equally between the spouses
The spouse who earned more income is solely liable
Each spouse is jointly and severally liable for the entire tax, interest and penalties
exp: Spouses who file jointly are jointly and severally liable for the full tax, interest and penalties on the return, so the IRS may collect the entire amount from either. Limiting liability to one's own income requires relief such as innocent spouse or separation of liability.

q: Ivy and Jake married on December 31 of the current year. Neither has any dependents. Which filing statuses are available to them for the current year?
choices: Single
Head of household
Single for one spouse and married filing separately for the other
Married filing jointly or married filing separately
exp: Marital status is determined on the last day of the year, so a couple married on December 31 is treated as married for the whole year and must file jointly or separately. Single status is unavailable to either spouse.
